tips.title: Every day: use the present simple
tips.body: With he, she or it, add -s or -es. After does or does not, use the base verb.
tips.example: He visits. Does he visit? He does not visit.

tips.title: Use the passage
tips.body: Find names, places and details in the passage before answering. You do not need to memorise every fact.
tips.example: The text says the Nile flows from south to north.

tips.title: Write about 50 words
tips.body: Cover the topic, use complete sentences, and check capitals and full stops.
tips.example: For an email, add a greeting, your message and your name.

tips.title: Happening now
tips.body: Use am, is or are with a verb ending in -ing for an action in progress.
tips.example: I am studying. She is reading. They are running.

tips.title: Read what is actually there
tips.body: Some passage topics do not match the lesson heading. Answer from the supplied passage.
tips.example: Wonderful Nile River has a passage about Omar visiting a museum.

tips.title: Nature words
tips.body: Review useful combinations: care for plants, pull out weeds, depend on the Nile, and protect yourself from the sun.
tips.example: We take care of our plants.

tips.title: Can and able to
tips.body: Use can plus the base verb. Use am, is or are plus able to and the base verb.
tips.example: I can run. I am able to run. She cannot swim.

tips.title: Jobs that help us
tips.body: Connect each job with what the person does.
tips.example: A paramedic helps patients in emergencies.

tips.body: The Proud Rose heading has sandwich and ice cream passages in this book. The questions test those supplied passages.
tips.example: John Montagu used bread and meat, according to the passage.

sections.passage: Ras Mohamed is a famous national park in the south of Sinai, Egypt. It is known for its beautiful coral reefs, colorful fish, and clear blue sea. People from all over the world visit Ras Mohamed to swim, snorkel, and dive. The nature in Ras Mohamed National Park is amazing. The park is home to many kinds of animals and plants. You can see sea turtles, dolphins, and many types of birds. There are also mountains and mangrove trees near the beach.

sections.passage: The Nile is the longest river in the world. It is about 6,650 kilometers long. The Nile flows through Egypt from south to north. It goes through the desert and brings life to the country. Many animals live in and near the Nile. Big fish like Nile perch and tilapia swim in the water. Crocodiles live in the river too. They are dangerous animals. Many birds come to the river to drink and find food. You can see kingfishers, herons, and ducks near the Nile. The Nile is very important for Egyptian people. In the past, the river flooded and brought good soil.

sections.passage: Hany has an ice cream shop in Cairo. He always walks to it. He opens six days a week. He never opens on Fridays. He makes the ice cream by himself. There are a lot of flavours in his shop. Most people like vanilla and chocolate. There is a museum across from his shop, so many tourists buy ice cream from his shop.

notes: This is a source-grounded revision bank from the uploaded Primary Six Performance Tasks and Assessment book (cover 2025/2026). It is not an official marking key or an exam-cutoff notice.
All numbered classroom and homework questions in printed pages 4–30 (PDF pages 5–31) are included. Optional oral warm-up discussion prompts are not counted as assessed items.
Unit 3 Lessons 4–5 and its unit review are extra practice: the observed Toddle answer-key label stopped at Unit 3 Lesson 3. That label does not confirm the exam cutoff.
Some headings do not match their reading passages. The bank keeps the actual passages and questions.
Open responses and writing are checked by a parent. Model answers are worked examples grounded in the passage, not an invented official key.
Spelling variants such as favourite/favorite, practising/practicing, and colour/color should be accepted in free writing when used consistently.
The Nile longest-river statement is assessed as a statement made by the supplied passage, without requiring a separate geographical claim.
Source numbering is occasionally duplicated, omitted or out of sequence; source labels preserve the printed question numbers.

Writing responses are original examples to compare after an attempt. Names and personal details in examples are illustrative, not claims about the child. Tasks with no printed word limit use a suggested practice guide.
